newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia protests spread but Milosevic stays silent.
newsitem.headline: Serbia protests spread but Milosevic stays silent.

text.p: Opposition protests gathered momentum across Serbia on Sunday while the autocratic President Slobodan Milosevic kept silent over demands that his government own up to alleged election fraud.
As Belgraders prepared to join demonstrations for the 28th day at 1400 GMT and students readied to march later in the afternoon, thousands demonstrated in several other towns.

Serbia's opposition and students have held daily street protests since the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition claimed it was cheated of victory in local elections in November in major towns and cities, including the capital Belgrade.
Milosevic has stayed largely silent apart from inviting a team from the the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) to look into the matter.
Diplomats believe this could be an opportunity for Milosevic to save face, but it remains to be seen whether he would accept an OSCE verdict -- whatever it might be.
Authoritative sources said Milosevic met Socialist Party leaders late on Friday to discuss the situation.

"One could easily imagine he had some harsh words to say. Not only did they lose elections for him, not only they were totally unprepared for the defeat but they also bungled the aftermath and tarnished his image," a Western diplomat said.
Despite the support by students and intellectuals and growing sympathy by many ordinary people, the opposition has so far failed to bring organised labour out onto the streets.
Even promised strikes by workers disgruntled by plummeting standard of living have failed to materialise.
"Milosevic is still by far the most popular leader in the country. The local vote was not so much for the opposition as it was against his local party hacks," the diplomat said.
"But if the opposition keeps up peaceful protests in the carnival atmosphere too long this could gradually change."
A Western political analyst commented: "Milosevic, set on becoming president of Yugoslavia with wide powers next year, did not need this hassle anyway."
To change the ceremonial powers of the federal presidency, Milosevic needs a two-thirds majority in the federal parliament to amend the constitution -- something he does not have.
On Saturday, more than 200,000 opposition supporters rallied in Belgrade in the biggest demonstration in more than three weeks of peaceful street protests.
In addition to the Belgrade demonstrations, thousands of people held protests in 17 major towns and cities.
A group of 17 students from the southern industrial city of Nis started a 230 km (145 mile) march to Belgrade on Sunday.
About 130 students from the northern town of Novi Sad finished a similar, 80 km (50 mile) march to the capital on Saturday, gathering support in villages and towns along the way.
